Anger can arise when an important goal is blocked, when you or someone you care about is attacked or threatened, or when power, status, or respect is lost.

## Words describing anger

Aggravation, agitation, annoyance, bitterness, exasperation, ferocity, frustration, fury, grouchiness, grumpiness, hostility, indignation, irritation, outrage, rage, vengefulness, and wrath.

## Prompting events and interpretations

Common prompting events include a blocked goal, events not turning out as expected, pain, attack, threat, or loss of power or respect. Interpretations can include believing you were treated unfairly, blaming, judging the situation as illegitimate, thinking rigidly *I'm right*, or replaying the event.

## Body changes, expressions, and action urges

Muscles, teeth, hands, or jaw may tighten; the face may feel hot or flushed; you may feel ready to explode. Urges and actions can include attacking, criticizing, throwing or breaking things, stomping, slamming doors, speaking loudly or sarcastically, walking out, brooding, or withdrawing.

## Aftereffects

Attention may narrow around the provoking event. Rumination, memories of earlier anger, imagined future conflicts, numbness, or dissociation can follow.

## When anger fits the facts

Anger fits when an important goal is blocked, you or someone you care about is attacked, hurt, insulted, or threatened, or the integrity or status of your group is threatened. Intensity also depends on the likelihood, importance, and effectiveness of the emotion.

## Acting on the urge, Opposite Action, and Checking the Facts

When anger fits and acting is effective, protect yourself, overcome a real obstacle, stop further attacks, or walk away from a threatening person. When it does not fit or acting would be ineffective, gently avoid rather than attack, take a time-out, do something kind, imagine understanding, and relax the body.
